#3597. Who Killed Fashion Founders Bryan Walker and Michelle Min?

Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkeley and Oakland. Each residence is worth millions; increase the amount for the occasional bit of newer construction. Unlike the busy urban streets below, the area is incredibly quiet. That’s one of the reasons everyone heard the shots.

“I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker. The couple, creators of the Bryn Walker clothing brand, were found just outside their residence around 10:45 a.m. on October 2, 2026, shortly after neighbors called 911 to report the sound of gunfire. Initial confusion about jurisdiction sent police from both Berkeley’s and Oakland’s departments to the scene.

By the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day. A firearm, he said, was located at the scene. He declined to offer further details on the case, saying that the department’s homicide division would handle the investigation.

Nearly seven weeks later, we still know next to nothing about how Walker and Min died. While OPD turned down my request to speak with Johnson, it sent me a press release with the same details he laid out on October 2. Follow-up questions were met with: “There are no updates being released other than the information below.”

Bryn Walker store on Vine Street in Berkeley, California.

“I don’t know what has publicly been shared or what privately has been learned about what took place,” Salzman says carefully. Police have been silent since the brief press conference the day the bodies were discovered. But Michelle Min’s brother, Paul Min, hasn’t been quiet.

Within two days after his 63-year-old sister was found dead, Paul spoke with outlets including the LA Times and the California Post, accusing his brother-in-law of killing his wife, then himself, following a series of disastrous financial decisions that led to significant losses and a collapse in his mental state. The interviews, given so soon after the crime, suggest Paul was still in a state of shock over his loss. Walker, who was 61 when he died, was “the most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known,” Paul told the LA Times. “I loved him like a brother.” Michelle “was utterly devoted to Bryan to the very end,” Paul told the Post, “and he shot her.”

After those interviews, which were published that first weekend in October, Paul fell silent too; I made multiple efforts to arrange an interview but was ultimately unsuccessful. But according to the Post’s interview, Walker “had quietly taken out loans against their properties, and had gambled on risky options and leveraged positions,” with estimated losses of “well over $100 million.” The debt, per the LA Times story, allegedly prompted Walker to suggest that he and the Min siblings “end things”—a proposal that alarmed the Mins, but only because of its implications for Walker’s mental health. Paul didn’t see Walker as a danger: “He said the idea that Walker would or could harm them was absurd to the two of them,” reported the Times.

The Mins came to the US from Korea in 1977, settling first near Kansas City. Michelle met Walker there in the 1980s, and after the Mins’ parents chose to move to California, the siblings, and Walker, followed. In 1992 the couple opened a clothing store in Berkeley that sold goods from other makers. As time went on, they began to manufacture more and more of their own goods.

Eventually, Bryn Walker evolved into a clothing brand known for loose linen looks with an Asian-meets-Swedish flair. “Flowy, a touch eclectic, made for perhaps older women who want to mesh elegant/sophisticated with a bit of boho uniqueness,” a longtime Berkeley resident told me over email. “Women who want to look expensive but with a bit of verve.” When I described the company to one San Francisco resident as “elevated Chico’s,” I got a stern look. “You better not let any of the Bryn Walker moms at Lowell hear you say that,” she said, referencing the city’s hotly competitive public high school. “These are not humorous people.”

Bryn Walker store on Fourth Street in Berkeley, California.

According to the Post piece, Walker “had stepped aside and allowed his designer wife to control their mutual business and his eponymous fashion label,” but it’s not clear when that management change occurred. As the brand grew, it struck a chord with fashion businesses across the country—from luxury boutiques to the family-run department store chain Dillard’s. Bryn Walker also opened its own brick-and-mortar storefronts beyond Berkeley.

Many of those stores are now gone. One Bryn Walker location in Santa Monica closed prior to mid-March of 2021, while a 22-year-old outpost in Palo Alto shuttered in 2020. On the East Coast, a shop in Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, went dark in 2024. A call to its shop in Vineyard Haven was met with a recorded message saying the business would be closed until further notice. That leaves just two company-owned shops, both in Berkeley, where Bryn Walker began.

One of those stores is on Berkeley’s buzzy Fourth Street, a glossy shopping destination lined with outposts of national brands like Apple, Lululemon, and Herman Miller. With items generally priced between $130–$300, it fits right into the overall ethos of that street—and Berkeley—where almost everything is spendy but not flashy; theoretically accessible, though not to those on a budget. During my recent visit to the shop, the sole staffer remained pleasant even after I identified myself as a journalist—but her tone grew firm. “It’s all still too raw,” she said of the tragedy.

I asked if, as he’d said he would in his Post interview, Paul Min had taken over management of the company following its founders’ deaths. “I don’t know about that,” she replied, before declining to speak further. I was told by another local business owner that Bryn Walker employees are actively seeking other employment; it’s unclear what will happen to the label now that its creators are gone. I tried to reach Bryn Walker management by phone and email for this story, but did not receive a response.

Emilie Raguso was one of the first journalists to report on the deaths, for her independent outlet, The Berkeley Scanner. As she began investigating, she “saw that the number of open shops was different based on where you looked,” she says. “I was getting this early inkling of what others later reported as far as the business being in trouble.”

“The writing was on the wall,” she continues, “but there was nothing explicit. It did seem like, Oh, this is not a thriving business.”

Paul’s comments to the media didn’t address the health of the business. Instead, he was focused on Walker and Michelle’s personal finances, which he alleged were laid to waste by Walker’s mismanagement. “Your spouse lied to you and lost over $100 million and you might be out on the streets,” Paul told the Post. “You might go from being one of the wealthiest people in the country to being homeless because your husband lied to you and wagered everything on crazy bets.”

According to Paul, things grew so grim for Walker that the Mins spoke about institutionalizing him. But it’s also unclear how they would have acted on that without Walker’s cooperation. California enacted its CARE Court program in 2023, more easily allowing court-ordered treatment plans for those who might pose a threat to themselves or others. But in practice, courts have been reluctant to take that drastic step, frequently rejecting petitions from those closest to the person in crisis.

Bryn Walker-Pacific Cotton store on Main Street in Vineyard Haven, Massachusetts.

Speaking with the LA Times, Paul said that in Walker and Michelle’s home, he “found a note that lists a couple of [mental health] facilities. I speculate he saw that note or somehow figured out she was going to institutionalize him, but I have no idea.”

Paul’s claim that Walker killed Michelle over snowballing financial fears isn’t out of the realm of possibility, even in a place as wealthy as the Bay Area. One year before Walker and Michelle died, almost to the day, entrepreneur Paula Truong fatally shot her husband, Thomas, and their daughters, Mackenzie and Alexandra, before hanging herself in the garage of their $2.2 million San Francisco home. Reporting found that the family had experienced a string of financial challenges, including several failed business ventures, a home foreclosure, and a number of unpaid debts.

But that was in San Francisco—a sometimes gritty city that people escape with moves to places like Panoramic Hill. “When you get up into the hills, it does feel like a world apart,” Raguso says. “It feels insulated from a lot of the more common disturbances and things that we deal with down on the flatlands.”

Salzman has lived on that hill for more than 20 years, and she’s still struggling with the notion that her neighbor might have killed his wife. “Bryan was very engaged with neighbors who were needing support that were near him,” she says, characterizing him and Michelle as “committed to the community.” But she also believes that the fear of losing wealth can drive people to desperate acts. “We see wealth as being both our greatest need and our greatest opportunity here,” she says, “and we are told that we will be happy when we consume. This is the message that we’re given everywhere we look”—especially in a region with more billionaires than anywhere else in the world.

Raguso isn’t sure why Oakland police are taking so long to announce the results of their investigation. “At some point, there would be a ruling,” she says, citing possible delays with the medical examiner’s office as a reason things haven’t been resolved. According to Salzman, the vacuum of information has inspired her to look at all her neighbors with a little more care. “Part of what I awoke to was how little I know about really what’s going on with people that I’m geographically so close to,” she says.

“I just would have loved for there to have been a way to be a part of showing up for them, even around the little things. The more people that are aware of what is happening, the more people are potentially able to heal.”

#3596. GTA 6 Nearing 25 Million Copies Sold And $2.4 Billion In Revenue On Day 1, Report Says; Take-Two To Reveal Official Sales Data Soon

The video game research company Sensor Tower has updated its GTA 6 sales tracker to reveal the latest, albeit unofficial, sales data for the open-world crime game. According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 reached 24.58 million total units via pre-purchases and copies sold at launch today--this works out to about $2.36 billion in gross revenue. GTA 6 is now available worldwide, so the numbers are expected to continue to climb higher.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick said on TBPN today that the company is going to share official sales data for GTA 6 soon, so it may not be much longer until we get some hard data directly from the source.

The report said PS5 sales are dominating the mix, with GTA 6 selling 18.44 million units on PS5 so far, compared to 6.15 million on Xbox Series X|S. That means of the 24.58 million GTA 6 sales so far, 75% are on PS5 and 25% on Xbox Series X|S.

In total, GTA 6 sales for PS5 have so far reached $1.77 billion in revenue, compared to $588 million for Xbox Series X|S. Sony and Microsoft keep about 30% of revenue due to their platform fees, so GTA 6 being a huge success directly benefits both of those companies.

The huge gap in sales between platforms is not surprising because the PS5 is dominating Xbox Series X|S in terms of console sales. In fact, GTA 6 is breaking records on Xbox, Microsoft has said, and the sales numbers for GTA 6 on Xbox line up with Xbox's share of the console market.

Sensor Tower projected as many as 25 million total pre-purchases for GTA 6 by launch, and that prediction is looking pretty accurate.

GTA 6 was the most preordered game of all time for PlayStation and Xbox.

Sony holds the marketing rights for GTA 6 on PS5, but that doesn't mean that Microsoft is doing nothing to try to promote the game. Just recently, Microsoft announced a GTA 6-inspired custom Xbox console that sits inside an alligator.

Circana has released new data that shows that GTA 6 holds 29% purchase intent among US console and PC gamers. That means nearly 1 in 3 console and PC gamers in the US plan to buy GTA 6–this is the highest purchase intent that Circana has ever measured for any game.

GTA 6 may indeed be a gigantic hit commercially, and one that helps lift the entire industry with increased sales of hardware and accessories. But anyone looking to buy a new console to play GTA 6 is set for major sticker shock, as consoles today are more expensive than ever. Not only that, but GTA 6 is not going to save the industry’s many serious and deep-rooted issues, experts believe.

GTA 6 launched on November 19 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. The game scored rave reviews, including a 10/10 from GameSpot. But Take-Two's stock price continues to take a beating this year. Not that it matters, though, because the stock is not the company, and the company is not the stock.

#3595. Andie MacDowell Praises Daughters Margaret, Rainey for Finding Their Paths

Andie MacDowell is relishing how daughters Margaret Qualley and Rainey Qualley have emerged as two of Hollywood’s most promising young stars.

“I love watching my kids and seeing that they’re not mini-mes,” the Four Weddings and a Funeral actress, 68, exclusively told Us at the Wednesday, November 18, L’Oréal Paris Women of Worth Celebration event recognizing extraordinary women leading grassroots nonprofit organizations and creating meaningful change in communities across the country. “They have defined themselves, and they are who they are, and they have strength and power in that. So I love that.”

MacDowell memorably worked with Margaret, 32, on the hit Netflix series Maid, with her daughter going on to land a Best Supporting Actress Golden Globe nomination for her command performance in body horror hit The Substance.

Rainey, 37, led the 2022 thriller movie Shut In and has since embarked on a flourishing music career. (MacDowell and ex-husband Paul Qualley share a son, Justin Qualley, who is not involved in the entertainment industry. She is also a grandmother of three.)

Asked how she encourages her children, MacDowell shared some gems of wisdom with Us, “I think finding who you are, being your authentic self, not curating who you are to please other people, but really being truthful and honest with who you are.”

The Golden Globe winner credited both of her daughters as having “done well” in Hollywood by following their own instincts.

“I love watching their creativity and the choices that they make, and just their creative spirits. They’re just highly creative individuals, and I love watching them grow,” she added.

While chatting with Us, MacDowell reflected on the “innate bond” she felt instantly with her three granddaughters.

“It happens automatically, which is really beautiful. They know you. They know you. It’s like they can sense it when you look in their eyes,” she said. “They know you’re part of them, you know. And I don’t know, it’s really special just having the opportunity to love your baby’s baby.”

With the holidays just around the corner, MacDowell revealed that her family have decided “not to have a lot of gifts” this year.

“We just want to have connection, bonding,” she explained. “But I do want to learn how to make marshmallows. … So that’s my goal.”

Next up for MacDowell on the career front is Beach Read, writer-director Yulin Kuang‘s 2027 comedy based on author Emily Henry‘s romance novel of the same name. MacDowell is part of an impressive ensemble that also includes Kevin Bacon, Bridgerton alum Phoebe Dynevor, The White Lotus‘ Patrick Schwarzenegger, Kristin Davis and Tig Notaro. (Beach Read will be released in theaters on May 7, 2027.)

#3594. These M5 MacBook Air Laptops Are up to $250 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple announced a slew of products in March, including the MacBook Air with the M5 chip, which ended up increasing in price in June due to the RAM shortage. These MacBooks come in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: In the leadup to Black Friday, Amazon is selling both at a $200 discount, and the 1 TB storage versions for $250 off.

Those discounts bring the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and $1,349.99 (originally $1,499.99) for the 512GB and 1 TB versions, respectively. The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,299 (originally $1,499), and the 1TB version is $1,549.99 (originally $1,799.99). All versions are at their lowest prices since the June price hikes.

The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Airs, the M5 base model has double the storage at 512GB. The powerful M5 chip makes the performance even smoother, according to Mashable's review. The aluminum design is as good as you'd expect from Apple's most popular portable laptop, lightweight and thin. It comes with a Liquid Retina display, Touch ID, a 12MP Center Stage Camera, and the Magic Keyboard.

Typically, the question would be whether to go for the slightly older M4 MacBook Air or pay a bit more for the newer M5 chip—but given how tough it is to find a new M4 laptop used, and the fact that most refurbished ones are the same price as the M5 with 512GB of storage, it makes the choice to go with the M5 a no-brainer—especially with a $250 discount.

#3593. Atlas Atelier Is Making Makeup for People Who Want to Be Remembered

You know how everyone is debating whether smoking is back? Atlas Atelier is like the subject of the makeup version of that conversation, in both its long, skinny lipsticks that evoke a cheeky cigarette and its past-bedtime, maybe something a little naughty is happening vibe. The Paris-based brand makes just lipstick, blush, and a black liquid eyeliner, all engineered to be best shown off at night, maybe under the light of candles, or as you sip a cocktail or wear a jacket with strong shoulders. It’s makeup that is supposed to look like makeup. Severe is not too strong a word to use.

The brand’s late-30s founder, Michelle Duncan, doesn’t smoke herself and doesn’t do barely there makeup along the lines of Rhode, Rare Beauty, or Glossier. “I am a New Yorker, and I’ve been living in Paris primarily for the last four or five years. When I arrived in Paris, everyone was so well-heeled that you would never see somebody wearing a gym look to go to dinner. This resonated with me about this idea of dressing up to go out no matter what you were doing, even if it’s going to a café. That was a huge inspiration for me,” she says.

Duncan knew the industry she was getting into. She’s a veteran of brands owned by Estée Lauder, including both MAC and Tom Ford Beauty, and she also worked for Cartier. Atlas Atelier—the “atlas” is in homage to Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged—just came out this fall in the US (now available at Violet Grey and Bergdorf Goodman). Vanity Fair spoke to Duncan about Paris expat life, rejecting celebrity brands, and what happens to makeup in unstable times.

The interview that follows has been condensed for length and clarity.

Vanity Fair: You know the challenges of the beauty industry. You’re not an influencer; you didn’t pick a celebrity to be the face of the brand or to partner with. Why not make it easier on yourself?

Michelle Duncan: Friends will ask, “Didn’t you want to do this with a celeb?” I wouldn’t want to. Culture and society is so focused on a quick buck right this second, which I’m totally into. I love making money very fast. This is so much about the world of Atlas, with the packaging and with the storytelling. The brand ethos of Atlas is about the night, about this seductive environment that, to me, will actually cut through the clutter in a long-term way. When a high-profile person launches a brand, the bet that they’re taking is on who they are as a person. For me, the bet is, do you buy into Atlas’s story?

Makeup has gotten very big and plastic and in some ways looks like toys. That was sort of my first remit on it. The whole brief was: We want to create something that looks like an object that you want to be able to keep. My inspirations really are the 1930s, the Art Deco, Paris moment, and how do we make it leap into the ’80s in some ways because that’s obviously also just a second extension of the ’30s?

The 1980s version of Art Deco is so good. All that lacquer and glass blocks and chrome lamps.

It felt like something that was radically different from what’s going on in the world right now, at least in beauty land. We’re exiting this no-makeup era, or hopefully exiting this quiet-luxury era. Those things were very pared back. Maybe focusing more internally about wellness and things like that. I understood that this was missing and that it was going to come back.

The idea of self-expression in a sort of glamorous way. In the 1930s, it was not a great time in the world. And if we remember, the 1980s in New York City was decadent and over the top and seemed very fun, but as a reaction to what was going on. I would argue that we are kind of in that place right now. We don’t really need to go into politics, but it is chaos right now. And so the answer to that is always this other form of self-expression.

The name of the brand is a reference to Atlas Shrugged. Are you a big fan of Ayn Rand?

I’ve always admired and been inspired by Dagny Taggart, one of the most iconic characters in 20th-century literature. She’s written as a fiercely independent entrepreneur in a male-dominated world, who is in control of her own life and embracing its complexity. When creating my business, I was trying to channel that vision of what a woman can be: intellectually formidable, professionally ambitious, and comfortable with her sensuality. I was especially struck by one moment in the novel, when Dagny draws on a statue using her lipstick, reminding us that makeup isn’t just to change our appearance—it can be a tool for women to own their own power. I wanted to create a makeup line that gave women that same feeling of confidence, ambition, and sensuality through tools like lipstick, blush, and eyeliner.

Yes. I have been wearing this winged-eyeliner situation for a very long time. Actually, since I was a teenager. If I don’t have my eyeliner on, I feel naked and I don’t feel like I have everything with me.

So you’re wearing eyeliner at home. What about the people who are reading this who may be thinking, I never go out, or I have kids, or I’m tired, or I work a lot, or all of those things? Do you want people to go out a lot? Do you go out a lot? Is it more just the mindset of going out at nighttime?

The idea of my brand is it should be a pleasure to put on makeup, and I want people to experience pleasure again and just forget about all of the things that are happening, like picking up the kids, or going to the grocery store, or getting the dry cleaning, or whatever it is. Just remembering what it means to have a nice time and be inspired by the night. I, on purpose and by design, did not launch foundations or these technical components of makeup, because that’s just not really what it’s about.

How is expat life? I know so many people who have moved to France, or they would love to move to France. What do you think that’s about?

In my social circle, it tends to consist of either people somehow in the fashion industry, the music industry, or the arts communities. A lot of those industries have just become quite commercial in America, as an example. And I haven’t lived in a lot of other countries, so I don’t really know expat life so well. But the amount of Italians that are here, the Spanish, the Germans, the Americans, and everyone just has this chaotic, frenetic energy of being around each other and doing things together. It’s pretty remarkable.

I know you’re not doing celebrity spokespeople, but who would you want if you didn’t have to think about money or access or if they already had a beauty contract?

Somebody like [the artist] Nadia Lee Cohen. She’s super glamorous. She’s quite creative. She’s a genius in a lot of ways, and she actually uses makeup as art. And then somebody like Dakota Johnson. I think she’s so chic now. Dua Lipa. I love her. She’s got the perfect energy for this. She’s there, she’s having a good time, and she’s powerful.

Do you want to expand into other products ? It feels like you could do a fragrance. Or maybe a very chic makeup remover?

I can’t wait for the day that we are able to launch a fragrance because that is one of those things you remember, along with lip color. You remember what they smell like, and when they leave the room, and so that’s the impression that Atlas is supposed to be giving—you’re remembered when you left the room.

What do Disney Parks, Make-A-Wish, and the Hallmark Channel all have in common? They love making dreams come true, and that’s exactly what happened for one teenage Hallmark movie superfan who has dreamt about being in one of the cable channel’s movies for a very long time.

Make-A-Wish partnered with Hallmark and Disney to make 14-year-old Ceci’s dreams come true, flying her and her family out to Disney World in Orlando, Florida, to appear in the upcoming Hallmark movie set at a Disney Park. Just like the film’s star Lacey Chabert, Ceci’s day started in the hair and makeup chair as the dedicated artists prepped her for a big moment. She was then decked out in new Christmas Disney Parks merch by wardrobe before being taken to set, where she not only got her own chair with her name on it, but also got a chance to meet with the cast of the highly anticipated Hallmark holiday flick.

Both Ceci and her mom got to appear in what is apparently one of the major scenes in the holiday romance film, titled Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True. They can be seen as hotel guests, sitting in the lobby of Disney’s Polynesian Village Resort holding Minnie Mouse and Dumbo plushies. I know I’m definitely going to be keeping my eyes open for the mother-daughter duo when the movie premieres as part of the 2026 TV Schedule on the Hallmark Channel on November 28th at 8 p.m. ET.

The excitement didn’t stop there, though, because Ceci also got a chance to step behind the camera alongside the film’s director. Not only did she get to learn what goes into directing one of Hallmark’s biggest movies yet, but she also got to yell “Action” on set. Watch:

A post shared by Disney Parks (@disneyparks)

Filming wrapped early this year on what could be Hallmark’s best Countdown to Christmas movie of 2026, but the magic hasn’t stopped for Ceci, who was surprised once again when her entire family was flown back out to Walt Disney World to attend the red-carpet premiere.

As if walking a red carpet as a teenager isn’t exciting enough, she also got to pose alongside the film’s star. I don’t know what I’m more jealous of: the fact that she got to walk the red carpet or that she got to see Chabert in her stunning Disney Princess-inspired gown. Probably both! Ceci stunned as well in a gorgeous burgundy gown that is perfect for the holiday season.

All of this is making me more excited for the film! Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True centers on Lindsey (Chabert), who plans to spend the holidays at Disney World with her extended family. In addition to having the best holiday ever, Lindsey also makes a wish at Cinderella’s Fountain for a love worthy of a fairytale to find her.

Enter Philip (Travis Van Winkle), a man Lindsey went on a disastrous first date with who just so happens to also be spending the holiday with his family at the “Most Magical Place On Earth.” As Lindsey and Philip’s paths continue to cross, sparks start to fly. It seems like Ceci isn’t the only one whose wish is going to be coming true.

Holiday Ever After: A Disney World Wish Come True premieres first on the Hallmark Channel on November 28th, but will be available to stream the next day on Hallmark+ and Disney+ with an active subscription.

#3591. Bruno Mars Announces Dad Peter's Death at 74: 'I Will Miss Him Everyday'

Bruno Mars is mourning the death of his father, Peter Hernandez. He was 74.

“Last week I got to hug my father one last time,” Mars, 41, wrote via Instagram on Thursday, November 19, alongside a photo of the musician embracing Hernandez in a hospital bed. “If you’ve ever seen me talk about him I’ve always said that he’s the man that taught me everything I know, especially when it comes to music.”

Mars continued, “He raised my four beautiful sisters, my brother and me. In my eyes he was the greatest dad in the world, and I will miss him everyday until we meet again. I love you, Pops. Kiss mom up there for me.”

Peter shared Mars and his four other children with ex-wife Bernadette San Pedro Hernandez, who died in 2013 at age 55. The former couple had divorced when the Grammy winner was 12 years old.

“My dad was just the king of finding these little spots for us to stay that we should never have been staying at,” Mars recalled on a 2016 episode of 60 Minutes. “We’d all sleep in one bed.

We had each other and it never felt like it was the end of the world.”

Mars noted that his childhood leant itself to the determination and tenacity it took to pursue a music career in Hollywood.

“Maybe that’s why I have this mentality when it comes to the music,” he acknowledged. “Because I know I’m going to figure … it out, just give me some time.”

Mars’ passion for music was apparent to Peter, who also was a performer.

“[Bruno] was a ham,” Peter mused to Midweek in a 2014 profile. “As soon as he could walk and express himself, he, like, had to be in the middle of everything and wanted to be a part of whoever he’d seen on TV.”

He added at the time, “Bruno is the product of a lot of love from all his family. No woman could ever love Bruno as much as his late mother did, and no man could ever love Bruno as much as I love him.”

Even with all the success Mars has achieved, Peter still saw the “Uptown Funk” crooner as his “baby boy.”

“I’m the proudest man in the world of Bruno Mars and his brother and sisters, and all the people who helped him get to where he is now,” Peter noted to the outlet. “I’m excited for him, for his sisters, for his brother. I’m so excited that I hope to be blessed with as much time as possible to see how far they go into the universe.”

#3590. Vanity Fair Announces New Hires and Promotions Across Departments

Vanity Fair Global Editorial Director Mark Guiducci today announced 11 new hires and appointments to the magazine’s masthead, deepening the magazine’s coverage across technology and politics, while adding talent to its operations and creative teams.

Vanity Fair’s new hires bring fresh perspectives to the magazine’s reporting on power and influence, alongside new creative voices to help shape its visual storytelling.

Maggie Coughlan is promoted to global managing editor. Since joining the team in 2021, she has held several positions at Vanity Fair, most recently as executive editor. She previously held editorial roles at the New York Post and People.com. She holds a master’s degree in digital publishing from NYU.

Emily Shugerman joins Vanity Fair as a senior staff writer reporting on wealth and politics on the West Coast. Emily comes from The San Francisco Standard, where she covered the shifting political allegiances of Silicon Valley’s richest, the fight over California’s proposed billionaire tax, and the growing power of AI lab workers. Before that, she was a reporter at The Daily Beast, where her investigations spurred leadership changes at national nonprofits and policy shifts at major corporations. Her work has also appeared in The Cut and The Guardian. She lives in San Francisco.

Jack Holmes joins as a senior editor for Vanity Fair, where he’s been editing features and political coverage since January. He will continue that work and expand into society and technology. Previously he was a senior staff writer and political editor for Esquire. He’s also the founder and publisher of The Football Weekend, a publication covering world soccer. Jack graduated from Vanderbilt University with a degree in philosophy and political science.

Nina Joyce is vice president of communications, based in New York, leading Vanity Fair’s communications globally. With 17 years of experience, she previously oversaw media relations for Condé Nast’s UK business and portfolio of brands, managing corporate reputation, brand strategy and major cultural events. Prior to joining Condé Nast, Nina spent a decade at Vice Media Group, holding senior roles across VICE, Refinery29, and i-D, and ultimately leading corporate PR across EMEA.

Roxanne Doucet joins as global visuals director. She has worked across New York and Paris, and collaborated with renowned artists and luxury houses including Dior, Loewe, and Balenciaga, building a practice rooted in fine art, documentary photography, and editorial storytelling. She was previously visual director at Vogue US and has consulted for Vogue France.

Dondre Stuetley joins Vanity Fair as senior visuals editor. Previously he was the photo editor at WSJ Magazine, commissioning stories on art, fashion, entertainment, design, food, and architecture.

Sameet Sharma joins as senior visuals editor. He was most recently the visuals director at V Magazine, and prior to V, he oversaw visual production at G-III, working on brands such as DKNY and Karl Lagerfeld. He also brings experience from Hearst magazines, where he worked on the photo teams at ELLE, Marie Claire, and Esquire.

Christian Zelaya joins as a senior designer. He brings more than five years of experience shaping editorial reporting into creative and clever visual stories for digital and social platforms and attracting readers for global brands like NBC, Forbes, and Scholastic.

Michael Kanyongolo joins Vanity Fair as audience development manager. He was most recently the news producer for Quanta Magazine, where he carried out web development, visual design, and production. He previously worked on web production at the New York Post and has a background in media and psychology.

Nazanin Hakim joins Vanity Fair as a creative producer on the video team. She brings a background in documentary filmmaking, having worked on a range of projects exploring politics, culture, and technology, including the Emmy-nominated series Turning Point: 9/11 and the War on Terror and What’s Next? The Future With Bill Gates.

Chris Black joins Vanity Fair as a contributing editor. He is a writer, photographer, and cohost of How Long Gone. He lives in New York and Los Angeles.

#3589. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

I don't know how you follow a $1.8 billion trip through Greek mythology, but Steven Spielberg apparently has an idea. Christopher Nolan is still taking a victory lap for The Odyssey, one of the biggest hits on the 2026 movie schedule, and the Jaws director just floated a follow-up I'd pay good money to see. The way he brought it up made me laugh, too. Even Hollywood legends know how to suggest another movie without sounding too pushy.

The moment came Tuesday, Nov. 17, at an awards-season screening of The Odyssey in Los Angeles. Spielberg moderated a Q&A with Nolan at the Directors Guild of America theater, where he praised the filmmaker's latest blockbuster before slipping in one more suggestion. As Gizmodo's Germain Lussier reported from the event, Spielberg told him:

The only other thing I want to say, not to challenge you or anything, but there’s always The Iliad.

I love how politely Spielberg slid that into the conversation. It's the cinematic equivalent of complimenting somebody's enormous Thanksgiving dinner and then asking what they're making next year. He even followed it up by insisting there was no pressure. Nolan, understandably, joked that Spielberg seemed to be speaking for Universal Pictures. Spielberg admitted the studio would probably appreciate it, but he was interested himself.

The idea makes a lot of sense. Homer's The Iliad takes place during the Trojan War, before Odysseus spends years trying to get home in The Odyssey. It wouldn't be a straightforward sequel, since we'd be going backward in the timeline, but the stories share a world. Imagine Nolan using his massive practical sets and IMAX cameras to tackle the conflict between Achilles and Hector. I'm already looking for a seat.

Here's what really makes the suggestion fun: Nolan almost got his shot at The Iliad decades ago. He was originally hired to direct Troy, the 2004 movie that eventually went to Wolfgang Petersen and starred Brad Pitt as Achilles. Nolan has since explained that he carried ideas from that unrealized project into The Odyssey, including the impressive Trojan Horse sequence.

Nolan has already explained why he chose The Odyssey. He considers The Iliad more grounded, while the later poem's monsters and stranger adventures offered something he hadn't seen done the way he envisioned. That doesn't mean he couldn't change his mind, especially after his latest movie has reportedly earned more than $1.8 billion worldwide.

There's also something delightful about Spielberg being the person to make this pitch. He helped develop Interstellar before Nolan took over, and Nolan consulted him while preparing Dunkirk. Watching Spielberg praise Nolan as a fellow filmmaker and then immediately ask for another movie feels like the most recognizable fan behavior imaginable.

For now, Nolan hasn't announced his next directing project. He told the crowd that he tends to focus on one film at a time and figures out the next one only after he's finished. So nobody should start booking tickets for The Iliad just yet. But if the man who gave us Jaws, Raiders of the Lost Ark, and Jurassic Park is personally asking for another giant Homer adaptation, I think somebody at Universal should at least write that suggestion down. Maybe keep the IMAX cameras handy.

In the meantime, The Odyssey is now available to rent or buy digitally, as well as on Blu-ray and 4K Blu-ray.

Amazon is offering early Black Friday discounts on like-new versions of its 2024 Kindles, with prices starting at $152.99 for the Paperwhite and savings of $27 to $75 across five models that include the color-screen Colorsoft and the pen-equipped Kindle Scribe. All five are a generation behind Amazon's current lineup: The company introduced redesigned Paperwhite and Colorsoft models (plus accessories) in October, with the new Paperwhite now starting at $199.99, and replaced the 2024 Scribe with a third-generation model in December 2025. As for its “like-new” label, it means these are pre-owned devices that Amazon has tested and certified to look and work like new.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite (16GB) is down to $152.99 from $179.99 and covers just about everything most people need for everyday reading, including enough storage for thousands of ebooks. Its seven-inch, 300ppi glare-free display is larger than the previous generation’s 6.8-inch screen, with faster page turns, an adjustable warm light, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. As PCMag notes in its review, it's a great option for readers who don't need color or handwriting features.

The Like-New Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $190.99 from $224.99, making it just $38 more than the like-new Paperwhite (16GB). For that relatively small difference, you're doubling the storage to 32GB and getting wireless charging, an ad-free lock screen, and a front light that automatically adjusts to your surroundings—on top of the same sharp seven-inch display, IPX8 water resistance, and up to 12 weeks of battery life as the standard Paperwhite, as noted by this PCMag review.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft (16GB) is down to $220.99 from $260.99 and offers something the Paperwhite models can’t: a color E-Ink display, which makes it well suited to comics, graphic novels, illustrated books, and travel guides. Its seven-inch screen shows that color content at 150ppi while keeping text at a sharp 300ppi, and you can mark passages in multiple highlight colors to keep your notes organized. That said, colors are noticeably more muted than on a conventional tablet, and battery life tops out at eight weeks, compared with 12 weeks on the Paperwhite.

The Like-New Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (32GB) is down to $243.99 from $287.99, making it just $23 more than the standard like-new Colorsoft. For that modest increase, you're getting twice the storage at 32GB, which is particularly useful for comics, manga, and graphic novels that take up more space than regular ebooks, along with wireless charging, an automatically adjusting front light, and an ad-free lock screen. However, as PCMag notes in its review, the color display produces more subdued tones than a conventional tablet, so the Paperwhite remains the more economical choice if you primarily read novels.

The Like-New Kindle Scribe (16GB) is down to $284.99 from $359.99, the biggest dollar discount in this roundup. Unlike the other Kindles here, it's built for reading and writing, with a 10.2-inch, 300ppi glare-free display and a Premium Pen with an eraser and shortcut button—making it the most versatile option for readers who want an e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3585. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang May Just Survive His Scandal

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Exactly three years ago today, the tech world found itself in an all-too-familiar crisis. On an otherwise ordinary Friday afternoon, the board of OpenAI abruptly fired Sam Altman, following a secretive deliberation about what was believed to be a pattern of deceptive behavior by the CEO. A shock wave of panic rippled through the industry: Employees rallied around Altman, who set up a makeshift war room in his Russian Hill home; investors made furious calls to the board to demand a reversal; and Satya Nadella offered to create the conditions within Microsoft for Altman and his loyalists to rebuild OpenAI from the ground up.

As the members of OpenAI’s board racked their brains for who might make a worthy replacement, the extent of their miscalculation quickly dawned on them. OpenAI could not survive without Altman, and the tech industry might not survive without OpenAI. Within four days of Altman’s firing (an event so fleeting that it came to be known as “the blip”), he was reinstated as CEO, and the board coup that failed to kill him only made him stronger.

Three years later, the foibles of a different man at a different AI company—Jensen Huang, who resigned from his post as CEO of Nvidia last week after the revelation of several compromising affairs—have thrown the industry and the stock market into tumult.

Not one to go down without a fight, Huang has reportedly hunkered down with his inner circle to plot his own comeback. Meanwhile, a petition to reinstate him, pending an independent investigation not unlike the one that exonerated Altman, has garnered nearly 200,000 signatures, including from the likes of Elon Musk, Travis Kalanick, and Garry Tan. Even President Trump has weighed in, noting that he “would certainly not mind” if Huang were reinstated. The news from today’s earnings report that the company had brought in a record-breaking $100 billion+ in sales last quarter under Huang’s leadership will only help their cause.

While an inside source told CNBC yesterday that Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang, the former executive is continuing to court public opinion independently. “I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said in a public statement Tuesday. “If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

It would be difficult to overstate Huang’s influence on the AI industry and US tech policy at large.

This entire mess has felt uncannily validating of the thesis behind Vanity Fair’s New Establishment list this fall, for which I wrote, “Never in the list’s history have the scale and the stakes of individual influence felt so high,” noting the “Ouroboros of investments and insular networks that make you realize how small and self-serving circles of power can be—and how quickly they could come tumbling down.”

We’ve officially entered the age of the too-big-to-fail CEO, in which our economy increasingly hinges on—and endlessly forgives—the moods and misdeeds of a handful of powerful men with few accountability structures. It’s not just the companies they founded that have become entwined with these founders. “The whole economy has basically been financed by Nvidia and in turn by Jensen’s ability to raise money,” says Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures.

Huang deserves a great deal of credit for having built his company from the ground up. But his trespasses—namely, becoming romantically involved with someone the State Department has linked to Chinese intelligence, and who has undeniably helped get America’s high-performance chips into the hands of our adversaries—are more than worthy of the scrutiny they’ve received.

Like a person who’s sick with a life-threatening illness but refuses to make a will, Huang demonstrated a staggeringly hubristic leadership. He had no real succession plan, installed a board and executive staff of yes-men and women, and created a “culture of omertà,” as his biographer, Stephen Witt, put it, that allowed his affairs to become an open secret within the company. Nvidia didn’t even protect itself with basic D&O insurance, which would have shielded it from the kinds of shareholder lawsuits it could now face. The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq have all continued their precipitous decline since the news of his departure was announced last week.

As a result, how many of us have found ourselves asking, Why should the fate of my 401(k) have anything to do with one man’s sex life?

If you need another example, consider Musk, who has gained almost single-handed control over our space and satellite infrastructure. At SpaceX, he’s also become a master of the newly popular dual-class voting structures that have allowed founders like himself and Mark Zuckerberg to consolidate control of their companies. On more than one occasion, his erratic whims have left our geopolitical fate hanging in the balance.

Perhaps start-ups do need these larger-than-life characters to get off the ground. As Rechtman puts it to me, “Great businesses don’t get built by committee. They get built by small groups of people and singular leaders. And necessarily, in the pursuit of some huge and lofty project, a person becomes elevated to the status of ‘great.’”

But as companies mature—and especially as they go public—they owe it to themselves and to investors to outgrow their founders. Plenty of the companies keeping our economy afloat, like Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, and Netflix, have indeed survived the parting of their founders.

Unfortunately, public markets are now falling victim to the same hype frenzy as VCs. AI-linked stocks now account for nearly half of the S&P 500, and 47 of those stocks made up three quarters of the index’s gains in the first half of this year. Nvidia, in one way or another, is connected to just about all of those companies through an intricate web of loans, partnerships, and investments.

So how do we deal with tech’s “great man” problem? This extreme concentration of power has helped foster a startling lack of resilience in our geopolitical and economic systems. But ask any antitrust expert, and they’ll remind you that it can also erode product quality, endanger consumer protections, and raise prices.

The answer cannot simply be for these men to improve their moral character, and it cannot be for us to become more forgiving. After all, any one of them could drop dead of a heart attack and leave us in the same predicament.

Walter Isaacson, the Silicon Valley biographer who is now interviewing many of the field’s “great men” on his new podcast, The Builders, believes the only possible answer “is to have more entrepreneurs who can build competing products, who can shoot off rockets and get them into orbit and create satellites and create chips and build fabrication plants.”

Rumors are already circulating that if he does not return to Nvidia, Huang may start his own competitive chip manufacturer, which helps explain why VCs are lining up to demonstrate their goodwill.

In the meantime, as we prepare for more mega IPOs, we would be wise to examine the structure of these deals to see what checks on power exist within these companies, from strong succession plans to empowered boards. Unfortunately, Anthropic is preparing super-voting shares for founders, which will give them decisive control over the company following its $1.4 trillion IPO. But hey, at least there are seven of them.

#3584. Jon Hamm's Wife Anna Osceola Gives Birth to Their 1st Baby, a Boy: Report

Jon Hamm and his wife, Anna Osceola, are reportedly parents after welcoming their first baby.

People reported on Thursday, November 19, that the Mad Men alum, 55, and the Confess, Fetch, actress, 38, welcomed a baby boy.

Us reached out to reps for Hamm for comment.

News broke in August 2026 that Osceola was pregnant after she was spotted showing off her baby bump in a bikini on a then-recent getaway to the Hamptons.

“Jon has always wanted to be a dad with Anna. Having a family was something that was really important to both of them from the beginning,” a source exclusively told Us later that month. “They’ve talked about this chapter for a long time and were always on the same page about wanting children, so for it to actually be happening now feels incredibly special.”

According to the insider, the Your Friends & Neighbors star was “over the moon” about becoming a dad and had been “so attentive and excited about every little milestone” throughout Osceola’s pregnancy.

“They’re both soaking it all in and are just so excited to become parents,” the source added to Us. “Their relationship has only gotten stronger, and they feel really lucky to be going through this together.”

Hamm and Osceola met in 2015 while working together on Mad Men. While Hamm starred as Don Draper on all seven seasons, Osceola joined the show for its final season, playing a receptionist named Clementine.

Despite working together on the hit period drama, Hamm and Osceola’s bond didn’t turn romantic until 2020, three years after they were briefly linked in 2017. Us confirmed in February 2023 that Hamm proposed to Osceola. The duo tied the knot later that year.

“Everybody I love was there. It was so emotional, and it felt right. I was like, ‘OK, I guess this is a thing,’” Hamm told The Hollywood Reporter in 2024 of their wedding day. “We did it [where the Mad Men finale was shot in California], which was also amazing. Again, it was like a reset, a reboot, a reframe, a reimagining, nine years later, almost to the day. So, it’s been great.”

At the time, Hamm also expressed his hopes to expand their family after previous indecision about becoming a father.

“I hope it turns into kids. It’s not lost on me that I’m 53,” Hamm stated. “I will be the old dad, but so it goes. It could be a good thing. We’ll see.”

According to Hamm, he never previously saw “marriage as a thing” until he met his now-wife.

“Obviously, my parents were not married long, so I don’t have a model to look at and go, ‘Oh, this is how one finds happiness.’ I just knew at a certain point I wanted to be with this person,” he told the outlet. “But when I proposed, I was terrified. I was like, ‘What am I doing?’”

#3582. Brandon Sanderson’s Mistborn TTRPG Solves the Biggest Problem With Licensed Games

The wildly ambitious campaign takes generations

The wildly ambitious campaign takes generations

Licensed tabletop role-playing games provide players with a new way to experience their favorite franchises like Star Wars, Star Trek, and the Lord of the Rings. But those adventures always come with a big question about how player characters are supposed to make their mark on stories that already have their own legendary heroes. Rather than erasing canon characters or turning them into quest-givers, the wildly ambitious Mistborn Legacy campaign for the Cosmere Roleplaying Game allows players to forge legends as powerful as any of Brandon Sanderson’s characters.

Sanderson has written seven Mistborn novels set between two distinct eras. The first trilogy exists in a bleak time when most of the world is uninhabitable. The immortal Lord Ruler crushes all dissent and brutally oppresses most people. The second series kicks off 300 years later at a time when the world has been restored and transformed into something resembling a blend of the Wild West and the Gilded Age. Mistborn Legacy spans both these eras as the PCs work to ensure the Lord Ruler can’t return.

Brotherwise Games’ designers worked closely with Sanderson and his longtime collaborator Dan Wells to devise a way for the players to really matter in the story of Mistborn. They take the historical view that the concentration of wealth and power is problematic in every era, whether that’s the nobles in Era One or the railroad barons and weapons manufacturers in Era Two. The players are always acting from a position of weakness as they try to uncover the machinations of powerful interests that could undo all of the progress the heroes of Mistborn sacrificed to make possible.

The campaign introduces the Eternity Spike, an artifact created through mass human sacrifice that could imbue someone with power that rivals the Lord Ruler. It cannot be destroyed and is actively pursued by a secret society. Era One strongly evokes the original trilogy, as players take on the role of a crew of thieves infiltrating high society and making allies of urchins and revolutionaries. There’s a whole scene where the players have to impress people at a secret masquerade ball and try to untangle a love triangle, but there are also tough fights against twisted monsters and killers trained to negate the players’ magical powers.

Era Two leans more into that series’ pulp adventure sensibilities. The Gilded Trio resemble Indiana Jones villains as they search for ancient secrets that can lead them to a lost magical artifact. Era One can get quite dark, and while Era Two has its own twisted villains, it’s a lighter adventure involving illegal street racing and spending time on a university campus.

The sections are connected by a legacy system, with hooks for the party at large and each individual character archetype. The characters become legends akin to Sanderson’s characters like Vin and Kelsier, so the game master takes notes on what they did at key moments as they inspire future fashion trends and build organizations that stand the test of time. The book is filled with “legacy moments” that create special conflicts or opportunities in Era One depending on whehter your character is a convict, urchin, or veteran. After completing the Era One adventure, players create new characters with connections to other players’ previous characters. For instance, the storyteller in Era Two is working on the convict’s biography while the rookie is inspired by the veteran’s heroism.

Both parts are meticulously detailed, packed with maps, character art, and subsystems for mini-games and downtime planning. There are also detailed handouts for everything from party invitations to newspaper articles. Getting a group together to play through a campaign of this scale requires commitment, but GMs and players are rewarded by an extremely rich world filled with plenty of ways to make a mark.

Mistborn Legacy is best run by someone familiar with Sanderson’s series, but there are so many character hooks that it would be easy for Cosmere novices to slip into the game world. Even if you’re not already invested in the story of Scadrial, it’s easy to empathize with heroes trying to fight oppression and ensure that the future is bright for everyone. Rather than making players feel like they’re walking in the shadows of the series’ protagonists, Mistborn Legacy lets them preserve what they built while forging their own legends.

#3581. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

#3580. 'Star Trek' Icon Patrick Stewart's Cause of Death Revealed

New details surrounding Patrick Stewart’s death have been revealed less than a month after the Star Trek icon died.

In a Los Angeles County Medical Examiner report obtained by TMZ on Thursday, November 19, Stewart died from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia at the age of 86.

According to the Mayo Clinic, Lewy body dementia is the second most common form of Alzheimer’s disease. The condition causes a decline in mental abilities that gradually gets worse over time.

Stewart’s death certificate also lists cardiopulmonary arrest (commonly called cardiac arrest) and a neurocognitive disorder with Lewy body, a progressive form of dementia that affects memory, thinking and movement.

Stewart’s remains were handled through alkaline hydrolysis, which is also known as water cremation, on November 3. The process uses water and chemicals instead of flames.

News broke on October 29 that Stewart had died. The actor was 86.

“He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” his spokesperson shared in a statement to Us. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

In lieu of sending flowers, Stewart’s Instagram account encouraged fans to donate to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.

Since Stewart’s death, the former X-Men star has been celebrated by his costars and friends in Hollywood.

Stewart’s widow, musician Sunny Ozell, has also paid tribute to the Hollywood legend on social media.

“The grief continues to come in waves. But I’ve also been experiencing such deep, profound gratitude. We left nothing unsaid,” Ozell, 47, wrote via Instagram on November 10. “He knew I loved him, and I know he loved me. Patrick and I truly, authentically saw one another, and we amplified each other’s best qualities.”

She continued, “I’ve been overwhelmed by the public response to Patrick’s death, and while I’m not at all surprised that he touched so many, I’m sincerely moved by the outpouring of sadness and loss. Thank you all for your condolences, they mean so, so much to me. My heart had to grow to contain my love for Patrick, and he changed me for the better, forever.”

#3579. Apple, Chase, United Outages: What’s Going On?

Read A Billion to One: From the mad scientists to the megadonors, a dispatch on the money, power, and influence of technology.

Every time I see a new headline about yet another system outage this week, the beat of “We Didn’t Start the Fire” starts playing in my head: “Microsoft, NSA, grounded planes from FAA / United Airlines, Chase Bank, can’t send funds on Apple Pay…”

It feels like I could write a parody verse a day at the rate our infrastructure is faltering. A few weeks ago I wrote about the spate of cybersecurity incidents that led the industry to label last month “Black October.” Now my phone is blowing up, with everyone from colleagues to high school friends asking, what the hell is going on out there?

Are we under attack by a rogue nation? Are outdated software systems suddenly all throwing in the towel? Is this all just cyber-business as usual, with an unusually on-edge public?

I’m inclined to believe it’s some combination of all of the above. The FBI issued an urgent warning today that bad actors have been using ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration testing platform, to attempt widespread attacks. A source at a financial services company tells me, “It’s been a miserable month…. Just constant probing and hacking attempts.” Companies—and especially government agencies—with outdated software systems are scrambling to patch these vulnerabilities, and are often unable to do so securely without taking their systems entirely offline.

“What used to take a skilled operator days or weeks of chaining is now happening in hours,” says Snehal Antani, cofounder and CEO of the cybersecurity firm Horizon3. In other words: With AI, bad actors can pretty easily jiggle every doorknob around the globe to see who’s left their doors unlocked.

Meanwhile, the total lack of clarity from the Trump administration hasn’t exactly been reassuring. Even one administration-aligned VC partner I spoke with this morning called the joint presser between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin a “clown show.”

For now, I’d urge you to heed the same advice I gave last time I wrote about this: Make sure those passwords are airtight and that multifactor authentication is activated. And maybe, just maybe, stock up on some light supplies you’d like to have around if 21st-century services stop working the way they’re supposed to.

“Going forward, expect this to become normal rather than exceptional,” Antani tells me. “We should expect persistent disruption of digital services—travel, banking, commerce, etc.—in the coming months as these organizations scramble to quickly improve their cyber resilience.”

$7 billion: That’s how much Sound Ventures, the firm founded by actor turned VC Ashton Kutcher and former music manager Guy Oseary, stands to profit from its 0.5% stake in Anthropic after the IPO this week.

Word is out that Elon Musk has invested a significant amount of money in Skydance, making him part-owner of the newly merged studio alongside David Ellison. With headlines suggesting the company may sell DC Studios and make other changes, I'm most concerned and have my eye on what the plan is for Star Trek.

It's been a tough year for Star Trek fans, despite it being the 60th anniversary. The year was marked by news that there are no new shows on the horizon, and ended with the passing of Walter Koenig and, of course, the death of Patrick Stewart. As the year ends, I have mixed feelings about what the future holds and how these two men may impact it in 2027 and beyond. Let's talk about it.

Ellison had a history with Star Trek before becoming head of the studio that owns it. Skydance helped co-produce both Star Trek: Into Darkness and Beyond alongside Paramount when they were separate studios, and he was on the record as a card-carrying Trekkie.

The CEO quickly mentioned Star Trek upon taking over Paramount in its original merger, and got the ball rolling on a new film. Unfortunately, we've seen this song and dance before with Paramount, as the issue was never developing a new Trek movie, but rather getting far enough along that it actually screens in theaters.

Additionally, Star Trek has zero shows in active development at this time. With no new announcements about any progress on that front, it feels as though the game plan is to let the final seasons of Strange New Worlds and Starfleet Academy air in 2027, and then maybe announce a new direction for the franchise. That's just an optimistic guess, however, as we've gotten no confirmation that is the plan.

Which brings me to the main problem I've had with David Ellison thus far. He's stated that Star Trek has a big role in what he wants to do with the future of Skydance, but we aren't really seeing any evidence of that. Right now, it feels like a lesser priority, something on the back burner, if you will, and I'm worried about just how long that will be the case.

Elon Musk's entry into Star Trek puts another alleged Trekkie at the top of Skydance's ladder, which could propel moves into happening sooner rather than later. For those who don't know, Musk is actually a canon figure in the universe, having been directly mentioned by Gabriel Lorca as one of the great minds of humanity. Despite his various movie and film appearances, Musk has never appeared in Trek.

As A Star Trek Fan I'm Eternally Grateful For What Patrick Stewart Did For The Franchise

He's also preached about recreating Star Trek in real life via his SpaceX company, but has simultaneously butted heads with other fans in interpreting what the series is about. We saw that when Starfleet Academy came out, and he openly joked about the show having obese actors and people wearing eyeglasses.

Perhaps he was not privy to Gene Roddenberry's view that looks wouldn't matter in an idealized society. It doesn't seem to be the only message he missed, as Musk has openly criticized the franchise's embrace of diversity and inclusion, two major principles Roddenberry stressed from the beginning.

I feel as though Musk loves the part of Star Trek that is about space exploration, especially with it matching his eventual goal for humanity to expand and colonize other planets. It's imperative, however, for him to also understand the bit that the series is a morality play, and without that bit included, it ceases to be the franchise that's thrived for 60 years.

Now, it's entirely possible David Ellison and Elon Musk keep their hands out of Star Trek, and entrust someone else to do what they think will make it most successful. As it stands right now, I have my apprehensions about either being too hands-on with it, but maybe I'll be surprised a year from now.

Star Trek remains available to stream on Paramount+. I'm waiting for those final seasons of Starfleet Academy and Strange New Worlds, and hoping that movie goes into production by the end of next year.

He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.
